# Statistical Analysis


```{r}
library(tidyverse)

ua_final <- readRDS("../data/ua_final.rds")
```

## Departure delay and Time of Day

Is there a simple correlation between departure delays and time of day?

```{r}
ua_final |>
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(hour, dep_delay)
  )
```


The correlation coefficient between scheduled departure hour and departure delay is approximately 0.203, indicating a weak positive linear relationship. This suggests that flights scheduled later in the day generally experience longer departure delays, although substantial variation exists among flights scheduled during the same hour.


During exploratory analysis, we noticed that flights leaving in the morning had less delays compared flights departing in the evening.

### Research Question:
Is there a statistically significant difference in mean departure delays between United Airlines flights scheduled in the morning (before 12 PM) and those scheduled in the evening (6 PM or later)?

Null hypothesis: Morning and evening departures have the same mean departure delay.
Alternative hypothesis: Mean departure delays differ between morning and evening flights.

Create our dataset for group comparision.
```{r}
time_of_day_comparison <- ua_final %>%
  mutate(
    morning_evening = case_when(
      hour >= 0 & hour < 12 ~ "Morning", # flights between midnight and 12  
      hour >= 18 & hour <= 23 ~ "Evening",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  drop_na(morning_evening)

```

Review summary statistics

```{r}
time_summary <- time_of_day_comparison |>
  group_by(morning_evening) |>
  summarise(
    total_flights = n(),
    mean_delay = mean(dep_delay),
    median_delay = median(dep_delay),
    sd_delay = sd(dep_delay),
    late_pct = mean(late) * 100,
    very_late_pct = mean(very_late) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

time_summary
```

Evening flight experiences average delay of 22.77 minutes compared to 4.61 minutes for Morning flights. There is a difference of over 18 minutes. 


Calculate observed difference in mean between evening and morning

```{r}

observed_diff <- mean(
  time_of_day_comparison$dep_delay[
    time_of_day_comparison$morning_evening == "Evening"
  ]
) -
mean(
  time_of_day_comparison$dep_delay[
    time_of_day_comparison$morning_evening == "Morning"
  ]
)

observed_diff

```

Simulate null distribution
```{r}

set.seed(5300)

N <- 10^4

perm_diff <- numeric(N)

for (i in 1:N) {

  # Shuffle morning and evening labels
  shuffled_group <- sample(
    time_of_day_comparison$morning_evening
  )
  # Calculate the difference in group means
  perm_diff[i] <- mean(
    time_of_day_comparison$dep_delay[
      shuffled_group == "Evening"
    ]
  ) -
  mean(
    time_of_day_comparison$dep_delay[
      shuffled_group == "Morning"
    ]
  )
}
```

```{r}
hist(
  perm_diff,
  breaks = 50,
  main = "Permutation Distribution: Morning vs. Evening",
  xlab = "Difference in Mean Delay (Minutes)",
  col = "lightblue"
)

abline(
  v = observed_diff,
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)
```


Calculate two-sided p-value
```{r}
p_value <- (
  sum(abs(perm_diff) >= abs(observed_diff)) + 1
) / (length(perm_diff) + 1)

p_value

sprintf("%.5f", p_value)
```

A two-sided permutation test was conducted to investigate whether mean departure delays differed between morning and evening United Airlines flights. The average departure delay was 4.61 minutes for morning flights and 22.77 minutes for evening flights, resulting in an observed difference of approximately 18.16 minutes.
After 10,000 permutations, none of the simulated differences was as extreme as the observed difference.

At the 5% significance level, we reject the null hypothesis. The results provide statistical evidence that mean departure delays differ between morning and evening flights, with evening departures experiencing longer delays on average.



## Departure delay and Wind Speed


```{r}
ua_final %>%
  drop_na(wind_speed) %>%
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(wind_speed, dep_delay)
  )
```
Weak positive correlation. 


We previously used wind severity low, medium and high to categorize wind speed. For statistical analysis we will group wind speed at scheduled departure time into two categories: Low (Less than 10mph ), ModerateHigh (10mph and higher). We are choosing 10mph threshold so we have an approximately even distribution of flights for low and higher wind level. 

### Research Question 1
Is there a statistically significant difference in the proportion of late departures (more than 0 minutes late) between flights experiencing wind speeds below 10 mph and those experiencing wind speeds of 10 mph or greater?

Null Hypothesis: The proportion of late departures is equal between low and high wind conditions.
Alternative Hypothesis: The proportion of later departures differs between low and high wind conditions. 

### Research Question 2
Is there a statistically significant difference in the proportion of very late departures (more than 30 minutes late) between these two wind-speed groups?
Null Hypothesis: The proportion of very late departures is equal between low and high wind conditions.
Alternative Hypothesis: The proportion of very later departures differs between low and high wind conditions. 

Create comparison dataset
```{r}
wind_comparison <- ua_final %>%
  drop_na(wind_speed) |>
  mutate(
    wind_group = if_else(
      wind_speed < 10,
      "LowWind",
      "ModerateHighWind"
    )
  )

wind_comparison |>
  count(wind_group)
```
Close to even distribution between high and low wind 


Review summary statistics
```{r}
wind_summary <- wind_comparison |>
  group_by(wind_group) |>
  summarise(
    total_flights = n(),
    mean_delay = mean(dep_delay),
    median_delay = median(dep_delay),
    sd_delay = sd(dep_delay),
    late_pct = mean(late) * 100,
    very_late_pct = mean(very_late) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

wind_summary
```
The two wind-speed groups contained similar numbers of observations, with 29,080 flights experiencing wind speeds below 10 mph during departure and 28,589 flights experiencing wind speeds of 10 mph or greater. Flights experiencing higher wind speeds had a slightly longer average departure delay (12.94 minutes) than those experiencing lower wind speeds (11.26 minutes). The percentage of late departures increased from 45.04% under lower-wind conditions to 48.93% under higher-wind conditions. Similarly, the percentage of very late departures increased from 12.37% to 13.89%.

Overall, the descriptive results suggest a modest association between wind speed and departure delays. Permutation tests will be used to assess whether the differences in late and very late departure rates are statistically significant.




```{r}
observed_late_diff <- mean(
  wind_comparison$late[
    wind_comparison$wind_group == "ModerateHighWind"
  ]
) -
mean(
  wind_comparison$late[
    wind_comparison$wind_group == "LowWind"
  ]
)


observed_very_late_diff <- mean(
  wind_comparison$very_late[
    wind_comparison$wind_group == "ModerateHighWind"
  ]
) -
mean(
  wind_comparison$very_late[
    wind_comparison$wind_group == "LowWind"
  ]
)


observed_late_diff
observed_very_late_diff

```
The observed proportion of late departures was 3.89 percentage points higher for flights experiencing wind speeds of 10 mph or greater compared with flights experiencing wind speeds below 10 mph. Similarly, the proportion of very late departures was 1.52 percentage points higher under higher-wind conditions.

Simulate null distribution for proportions of late and very late flights

```{r}
set.seed(5300)

N <- 10^4

# Store simulated differences for each outcome
perm_late_diff <- numeric(N)
perm_very_late_diff <- numeric(N)

for (i in 1:N) {

  # Randomly shuffle wind group labels
  shuffled_group <- sample(wind_comparison$wind_group)

  # Difference in proportion of late departures
  perm_late_diff[i] <- mean(
    wind_comparison$late[
      shuffled_group == "ModerateHighWind"
    ]
  ) - mean(
    wind_comparison$late[
      shuffled_group == "LowWind"
    ]
  )

  # Difference in proportion of very late departures
  perm_very_late_diff[i] <- mean(
    wind_comparison$very_late[
      shuffled_group == "ModerateHighWind"
    ]
  ) - mean(
    wind_comparison$very_late[
      shuffled_group == "LowWind"
    ]
  )
}
```

Calculate P-values

```{r}
p_late <- (sum(abs(perm_late_diff) >= abs(observed_late_diff)) + 1) / (N + 1)

p_very_late <- (sum(abs(perm_very_late_diff) >= abs(observed_very_late_diff)) + 1) / (N + 1)

# Display results

sprintf("%.5f", p_late)
sprintf("%.5f", p_very_late)

```

```{r}
sum(abs(perm_late_diff) >= abs(observed_late_diff))

sum(abs(perm_very_late_diff) >= abs(observed_very_late_diff))
```
```{r}
mean(perm_late_diff)
mean(perm_very_late_diff)
```
Two-sided permutation tests were conducted to investigate differences in late and very late departure rates between flights experiencing wind speeds below 10 mph and those experiencing wind speeds of 10 mph or greater. The proportion of late departures was 3.89 percentage points higher under higher-wind conditions, while the proportion of very late departures was 1.52 percentage points higher.
After 10,000 permutations, neither test produced a simulated difference as extreme as its observed difference. The estimated p-value was approximately 0.0001 for both tests.
At the 5% significance level, we reject both null hypotheses. The results provide statistical evidence of differences in late and very late departure proportions between the two wind-speed groups.


## Departure Delay and Precipitation


```{r}
ua_final %>%
  drop_na(precip) %>%
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(precip, dep_delay)
  )
```
There is a weak correlation between precipitation and departure delays. 



```{r}
precip_test <- ua_final%>%
  drop_na(precip) %>%
  mutate(wet_dry = if_else(precip > 0, "Wet", "Dry"))

precip_test %>%
  group_by(wet_dry) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    late_rate = mean(late),
    very_late_rate = mean(very_late),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

During exploratory analysis we found that the percentage of flight late and very late was higher when there was percipitaiton (wet conditions) versus when there was no precipitation (dry conditions).

### Research Question 1
Is there a statistically significant difference in the proportion of late departures (more than 0 minutes late) between flights experiencing precipitation (wet conditions) and those experiencing dry condition?

Null Hypothesis: The proportion of late departures is equal between dry (where there is no precipitation) and wet conditions (where there is any precipitation).
Alternative Hypothesis: The proportion of late departures differs between dry and wet conditions. 

### Research Question 2
Is there a statistically significant difference in the proportion of very late departures (more than 30 minutes late) between flights experiencing precipitation (wet conditions) and those experiencing dry condition?

Null Hypothesis: The proportion of very late departures is equal between dry (where there is no precipitation) and wet conditions (where there is any precipitation).
Alternative Hypothesis: The proportion of very late departures differs between dry and wet conditions.



```{r}
observed_precip_late_diff <- mean(
  precip_test$late[
    precip_test$wet_dry == "Wet"
  ]
) -
mean(
  precip_test$late[
    precip_test$wet_dry == "Dry"
  ]
)


observed_precip_very_late_diff <- mean(
  precip_test$very_late[
    precip_test$wet_dry == "Wet"
  ]
) -
mean(
  precip_test$very_late[
    precip_test$wet_dry == "Dry"
  ]
)


observed_precip_late_diff
observed_precip_very_late_diff
```
The observed proportion of late departures was 17.70 percentage points higher for flights experiencing wet conditions compared with flights departing during dry. Similarly, the proportion of very late departures was 12.55 percentage points higher under wet conditions.

Simulate null distribution of late vs very late flights during wet and dry conditions. 

```{r}
set.seed(5300)

N <- 10^4

# Store simulated differences for each outcome
perm_precip_late_diff <- numeric(N)
perm_precip_very_late_diff <- numeric(N)

for (i in 1:N) {

  # Randomly shuffle Wet-Dry labels
  shuffled_group <- sample(precip_test$wet_dry)

  # Difference in proportion of late departures
  perm_precip_late_diff[i] <- mean(
    precip_test$late[
      shuffled_group == "Wet"
    ]
  ) - mean(
    precip_test$late[
      shuffled_group == "Dry"
    ]
  )

  # Difference in proportion of very late departures
  perm_precip_very_late_diff[i] <- mean(
    precip_test$very_late[
      shuffled_group == "Wet"
    ]
  ) - mean(
    precip_test$very_late[
      shuffled_group == "Dry"
    ]
  )
}
```


Calculate p-value

```{r}
p_precip_late <- (sum(abs(perm_precip_late_diff) >= abs(observed_precip_late_diff)) + 1) / (N + 1)

p_precip_very_late <- (sum(abs(perm_precip_very_late_diff) >= abs(observed_precip_very_late_diff)) + 1) / (N + 1)

# Display results

sprintf("%.5f", p_precip_late)
sprintf("%.5f", p_precip_very_late)

```

Two-sided permutation tests were conducted using 10,000 permutations to investigate whether the proportions of late and very late departures differed between wet and dry conditions. The observed proportion of late departures was 17.70 percentage points higher during wet conditions, while the proportion of very late departures was 12.55 percentage points higher. 
Both tests produced estimated p-values of approximately 0.0001. At the 5% significance level, we reject both null hypotheses. The results provide strong statistical evidence that late and very late departure rates differ between wet and dry conditions, with higher observed rates during wet conditions.

## Departure Delay and Time of Year

During exploratory data analysis, we observed that departure delays varied across months, with particularly high delay rates during June, July, and December. 

To investigate seasonal differences, group flights into summer (June–August) and winter (December–February) categories.
### Research Question 1
Is there a statistically significant difference in the proportion of late departures (more than 0 minutes late) between flights in summer months (June-August) and winter months (December-February?

Null Hypothesis:The proportion of late departures is equal between summer and winter.
Alternate Hypothesis: The proportion of late departures differs between summer and winter.


### Research Question 2
Is there a statistically significant difference in the proportion of very late departures (more than 30 minutes late) between flights in summer months (June-August) and winter months (December-February?

Null Hypothesis:The proportion of very late departures is equal between summer and winter.
Alternate Hypothesis: The proportion of very late departures differs between summer and winter.


Create our dataset of analysis

```{r}

time_of_year_comparison <- ua_final %>%
  mutate(
    summer_winter = case_when(
      month %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "Summer", # Assign Summer label if month is 6,7,8
      month %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter", # Assign Winter label if month is 12,1,2
      TRUE ~ NA_character_ # Since there are other months, we assign "NA"
    )
  ) %>%
  drop_na(summer_winter) # Filter out observation for other than summer or winter
```


Capture observed values
```{r}
observed_season_late_diff <- mean(
  time_of_year_comparison$late[
    time_of_year_comparison$summer_winter == "Summer"
  ]
) -
mean(
  time_of_year_comparison$late[
    time_of_year_comparison$summer_winter == "Winter"
  ]
)

observed_season_very_late_diff <- mean(
  time_of_year_comparison$very_late[
    time_of_year_comparison$summer_winter == "Summer"
  ]
) -
mean(
  time_of_year_comparison$very_late[
    time_of_year_comparison$summer_winter == "Winter"
  ]
)

observed_season_late_diff
observed_season_very_late_diff
```
Simulate null distribution

```{r}
set.seed(5300)

N <- 10^4

perm_season_late_diff <- numeric(N)
perm_season_very_late_diff <- numeric(N)

for (i in 1:N) {

  # Shuffle summer/winter labels
  shuffled_group <- sample(
    time_of_year_comparison$summer_winter
  )

  # Difference in late proportions
  perm_season_late_diff[i] <- mean(
    time_of_year_comparison$late[
      shuffled_group == "Summer"
    ]
  ) -
  mean(
    time_of_year_comparison$late[
      shuffled_group == "Winter"
    ]
  )

  # Difference in very late proportions
  perm_season_very_late_diff[i] <- mean(
    time_of_year_comparison$very_late[
      shuffled_group == "Summer"
    ]
  ) -
  mean(
    time_of_year_comparison$very_late[
      shuffled_group == "Winter"
    ]
  )
}
```


Calculate p-value
```{r}
p_season_late <- (
  sum(abs(perm_season_late_diff) >=
      abs(observed_season_late_diff)) + 1
) / (N + 1)

p_season_very_late <- (
  sum(abs(perm_season_very_late_diff) >=
      abs(observed_season_very_late_diff)) + 1
) / (N + 1)

sprintf("%.5f", p_season_late)
sprintf("%.5f", p_season_very_late)
```
Two-sided permutation tests were conducted using 10,000 permutations to investigate if the proportions of late and very late departures differed between summer months and winter months. The observed proportion of late departures was 2.48 percentage points higher during summer compared with winter. Similarly, the proportion of very late departures was 5.04 percentage points higher during summer.
Both permutation tests produced estimated p-values of approximately 0.0001. At the 5% significance level, we reject both null hypotheses. The results provide statistical evidence that the proportions of late and very late departures differ between summer and winter, with higher observed rates during summer.
